headline: Marine Parkway Bridge After Dark: Slot Bass on the Outgoing, Fluke Rule the Day
subhead: Warm bay water has flipped the striper switch to nighttime — but fluke, schoolies, and a rebuilding weakfish bite keep the rods bent from sunup to sundown.
body_markdown:
I picked the bridge this week, not the boat. When the bay water gets this warm — shallow flats baking all afternoon, the channels holding heat overnight — the keeper bass stop feeding on my schedule and start feeding on theirs. That means Marine Parkway. I can walk out on the pilings, fish the pilings and riprap on the Rockaway side, and be home by midnight instead of running the boat back across the bay in the dark. Access matters as much as tackle out here, and right now the access that pays is a rod holder on the bulkhead at 10 p.m., not a rod holder at noon.

Two nights out of three this week I had bass on the outgoing at the bridge — not a pile of them, but real fish, low 20s up to one push-30 that I measured twice before I let her go. Bucktails in white, 1.5 to 2 ounce, bounced off the bottom along the current seam where the tide funnels under the span, worked best. A couple guys were soaking eels on the drift and doing fine too. The pattern's simple: the water's been sitting in the high 70s across the flats all day, the bass don't want to burn energy chasing bait in that soup, so they slide out to the bridge and the deeper cuts near the inlet mouth after dark when things cool a few degrees and the current gets moving. If you're daytime-only, you're mostly fishing for schoolies and snapper blues inside the bay right now, and that's fine — it's just a different game.

Speaking of that different game — fluke have been the steadier daytime bite all month, and this week didn't change that. Cross Bay Bridge channel edges, the flats off Ruffle Bar, and the deeper holes around Motts Basin have all given up fish on the drift, five to six-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, teased with a Bonito strip if you've got it. Best window is the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide, when bait gets pushed up onto the edges and the fluke stack up to ambush it. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of shorts, but enough 18-to-20-inch fish mixed in to make it worth the drift time. I had four keepers Tuesday morning working the flats in 8 to 12 feet off Ruffle Bar, all on the incoming.

The other thing worth talking about — we flagged last week that the weakfish bite would start rebuilding as the bay kept warming on calm evenings, and that's exactly what's happening. Grassy Bay and the channel edges near the JoCo Marsh have been giving up weakfish in the last hour of daylight into dusk, mostly on light jigs tipped with a sandworm or a small piece of bloodworm, fished slow along the bottom where the mud drops into the channel. Nothing giant — most are in that 16 to 18-inch range — but a legal weakfish on a calm July evening in this bay is still a good fish, and it's a sign the bay's settling into a healthier summer rhythm.

For the kayak crowd, this is prime time to work the flats inside — launch out of Canarsie Pier or the Sebago Canoe Club ramp and paddle the shallow grass edges for schoolie bass and snapper blues on topwater or small metal. It's not trophy fishing, but it's steady action for kids and for anyone who just wants bent rods without the boat traffic.

On the ocean side, there's bunker showing along the beach from Rockaway down toward Breezy Point, and where there's bunker there's usually blues working them from below. I'd check the inlet itself on a strong outgoing — the current pulls bait past the jetty and I've seen blues follow it right through the cut. Cast bucktails or diamond jigs into the moving water at the mouth, especially around the second half of the ebb when everything funnels through that gut. It hasn't been the wall-to-wall blitz you're hearing about up the Jersey beaches, but it's there if you're willing to work the tide right.

Looking ahead — we're heading into the July 21 neap, which is going to soften the current everywhhere from the bridge to the inlet. That's usually bad news for anyone depending on a hard-running rip, but it can widen the productive window for slower presentations like eels and light bucktails, since the fish aren't getting blown off structure by a screaming tide. I'd expect the bass pattern at the bridge to hold through the week, maybe even extend a little later into the evening as the current eases. Fluke should stay consistent on the flats regardless of moon phase — that bite's been the most dependable thing in the bay all month. And if this bunker push along the beach keeps building the way it has to our north, don't be shocked if Rockaway starts seeing real blitz activity in the surf before the month's out. I'll be watching Breezy Point close for that.
